title: Screen Score Foundations: Leitmotif, Diegesis & Underscore
welcome_lead: Discover how music tells stories on screen — from leitmotifs to diegetic sound.
meta_desc: GCSE Music Film & Game Music Adventure 1: foundations of leitmotif, diegetic vs non-diegetic, underscore and mickey-mousing.

concepts.def: Short theme linked to a character or idea (Wagner, Williams).
Music characters can hear (a radio on screen).
Music only the audience hears — the underscore.
Background music supporting a scene's mood.
Music matching on-screen action exactly (often comedic).
Main recognisable tune of a film or game.

walkthroughs.body_html:
A leitmotif is a short musical idea linked to a character, place or emotion. Wagner pioneered it in his operas; John Williams made it iconic in Star Wars (1977) with themes for Luke, Vader, the Force and more.

The same motif can be developed — minor for sadness, fast for action, distorted for danger — to tell the story without words.

Diegetic music exists in the film world — a band in a bar, a song on the car radio. Characters can hear it.

Non-diegetic music is the underscore — only the audience hears it. It guides our emotions without the characters knowing it's there.

Named after early Disney cartoons, mickey-mousing matches each on-screen movement with a musical gesture — footsteps as pizzicato strings, a slip as a slide whistle.

Effective in comedy and animation, but used sparingly in serious drama, where underscore usually paints mood instead.
